name: Carlos Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a tiny translation co-op with my friend Priya, just the two of us, out of a shared office above a bike shop. We translate websites, campaign leaflets and grant reports between Danish, English and Spanish, mostly for charities, housing groups and a couple of food co-ops. My day starts with AI drafts of whatever came in overnight, then I spend hours rewriting them so they sound like real people and not a brochure. Afternoons are calls with clients, which I actually enjoy.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Grant deadlines. Every charity in the city seems to apply for the same fund in the same week, and suddenly we're translating forty pages by Friday. And clients who think 'the AI does it' means it should be free. I spend a lot of time explaining that the machine gives you words, and I give you a voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: these tools are good assistants and bad authors. I'd post a little thread about how we use them at the co-op, because people are curious. And I'd still argue that translators should be paid properly for the human part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is a comfortable world for me. The AI already does the dull first draft, and if it stops improving, my editing and my client relationships stay valuable. Priya and I would be fine, maybe better than fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing the co-op, maybe take on a third member, someone just out of university. I'd keep tuning how we use the tools so our drafts are faster. And I'd put some of the co-op's profit into a proper pension for both of us, because we've never done that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit relieved for my friends who don't use the tools. They'd have time to catch up. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI is already part of your day. Wouldn't a plateau feel like a letdown?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, honestly. I like new toys and I'd be curious what came next. But a world where my job stays interesting and my friends keep theirs is not something I'd complain about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hire that third person and pay them properly, which matters to me politically. A co-op that only works because it underpays its newest member isn't a co-op. Then a holiday, because I haven't taken one in two years.

I'd argue translators deserve **proper pay** for the human part of the work.
think: I think this is a **comfortable world** for me and the co-op.
My **editing and client relationships** stay valuable if the tools stop improving.
do: Hire a **third member** fresh out of university.
Keep tuning the co-op's **AI workflow** for faster drafts.
Set up **pensions** for Priya and himself from co-op profit.
feel: He feels **calm** and relieved for colleagues who don't use the tools.

fieldNote: He already uses AI **every day** and sees it as an assistant.
His **co-op values** shape spending choices, like paying a new hire fairly.
He admits a small **disappointment** that the technology stalled.

steps.text: Hire a third co-op member on a fair salary
Keep refining the co-op's AI drafting routine
Set up pensions for Priya and himself from co-op profit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for unions and co-ops to step up, not to sulk. If AI is taking writing and checking work, the profits should be shared with the workers whose texts trained it. I'd be at the union meetings arguing for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the co-op would be squeezed, because charities would try doing their own translations with free tools. We'd lose maybe a third of our work. But I already know these tools better than most, so I'd probably land the clients who want it done properly and fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start selling a new service: setting up AI translation for small charities, then checking the output for them every month. I'd learn more of the technical side, like building glossaries the tools can use. And I'd push the translators' union to run free AI training for members who are behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, which feels a bit guilty to say. I'd be worried for older translators and for the friends who refused to touch any of it. For me it feels like a door opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited and also worried for others. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excitement for me, worry for them, both at once. I don't think that's a contradiction. That's why I'd push the union, because my luck isn't a policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my co-op partner Priya we stop selling words and start selling trust. Charities don't need someone to type a translation any more; they need someone they can call when the machine gets their housing leaflet wrong. We become that someone.

say: I'd say **unions and co-ops** should step up, not sulk.
I'd argue **profits** should be shared with workers whose texts trained the AI.
think: I think charities doing their own work would cost the co-op about **a third** of jobs.
My skill with the **tools** would probably win the clients who want quality.
do: Sell a new service **setting up AI translation** for small charities.
Learn to build **glossaries** that the AI tools can use.
Push the union to run **free AI training** for members.
feel: He feels **excited**, with some **guilt** about colleagues left behind.
S1.quote: I'd tell my co-op partner Priya we stop selling words and start selling trust.
fieldNote: He sees the shift as a **door opening** for himself, not a threat.
His progressive politics show in pushing **shared gains** and union training.
His mood is **uneasy** because the co-op loses work but his income looks safe.

steps.text: Launch a monthly AI translation setup-and-check service for charities

Ask the union to run free AI training for members

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income or something like it, and we need it before the layoffs, not after. I'd be blunt online that the companies building this should be taxed to pay for it. And I'd say that even as someone who uses AI every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my translation work disappears in this one, maybe within a year of AGI. My edge was knowing the tools better than others, and that edge vanishes when the tool needs nobody. The robots coming three years later don't change much for me, because I don't do anything hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Priya the first month and decide what the co-op becomes. I'd guess we'd run in-person workshops for charities and migrant groups on using AI safely, which needs a human in the room for a while. I'd keep our savings untouched as long as possible and join whatever political movement pushes for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, really nervous, though I'd hide it behind jokes. I've always been the one who saw change coming and liked it. In this picture I'd be as lost as everyone else, just with better software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. Do you really think the co-op survives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, as something different. Not as a translation shop. If it survives, it's because people still want a face to talk to while everything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office above the bike shop. We could work from my flat and save the rent. The pension contributions would go on pause too, which would sting, because we only just started them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's enough to build protections if we stop arguing about whether it's real. I'd be pushing the union to negotiate transition funds with the big agencies now. And I'd be loud about a basic income pilot in our city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to change shape properly. The translation work fades over the first three years, and I'd use that to build the next thing while it still pays. I think I'd be fine, but I'd be watching closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the workshops for charities in the first year while the translation work still covers the bills. I'd take an evening course in community organising, maybe through the union, because that's where I think I'd end up. And I'd keep a year of savings ring-fenced for the switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Edgy, but awake. It's the kind of pressure that makes me work better. I'd still have some nights where I stare at the ceiling, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How sure are you that the workshops idea lasts until 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not sure at all. The workshops are a bridge, not a destination. The real destination is organising, helping people in their actual neighbourhood, which needs bodies in rooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger translators at the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the AI tools now, but don't fall in love with them. And join the union this week, not when the email comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd talk about using the decade to build public retraining and stronger unions. Online, I'd probably be the optimist in every argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd keep translating and running the co-op for six or seven years, and I'd enjoy it. I'd have plenty of warning when it starts to fade. My worry is more for the field than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the co-op slowly, hire that third member, and add AI setup work for charities as a second line. I'd finish a part-time degree in community development by about 2031. And I'd keep putting money in a pension, which feels strange in this picture, but I'd do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. There's a small voice saying the end of translation is still the end of translation. But I'd have time to choose, which is all I really want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you more relaxed than you should be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'm good at believing I'll adapt in time. Priya would keep me honest, she's the worrier between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running some kind of neighbourhood project, still using three languages, probably with AI doing the paperwork. Less money than now, maybe. More people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my usual trick of being early wouldn't work. What would help is a basic income, or at least a guaranteed bridge, plus the companies paying into a fund for people whose work trained their tools. Unions with real power would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who owns the tools. If co-ops and unions owned some of the AI tools, this would feel very different. Right now a few companies decide what my next ten years look like.

headlineQuote: If co-ops and unions owned some of the AI tools, this would feel very different. Right now a few companies decide what my next ten years look like.
portrait: Carlos is a 27-year-old translator who runs a **two-person co-op** with his friend Priya.
He uses AI **every day** and sees it as a good assistant but a bad author.
He's left-leaning and pushes **unions, basic income** and taxing AI companies.
In mild pictures he expects to **gain clients**; in the AGI pictures his edge disappears.
His long-term plan points toward **community organising** in three languages.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because **being early** to new tools would no longer help.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or guaranteed bridge, and a fund paid by companies whose tools used translators' work.
